extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of Plato's Republic; scholars and readers of classical political philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Normative standards drawn from Plato's Republic (Books V–VI) describing how an ideal city should treat enemies and internal disputes, how heroes are to be honoured, and the character, abilities, and education required of guardians/philosopher-rulers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honouring the brave
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Homer shall be our teacher; and we too, at sacrifices and on the like occasions, will honour the brave according to the measure of their valour, whether men or women, with hymns and those other distinctions which we were mentioning; also with “seats of precedence, and meats and full cups;”’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Honours (hymns, precedence, feasting) are both tribute and training: public praise strengthens and cultivates courage. Use praise appropriate to valour; see this as a pedagogic instrument rather than mere flattery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funeral honours for heroic and pre-eminent goodness
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who die gloriously in war or who are deemed pre-eminently good shall receive special sepulture and honours; Hesiod's authority is appealed to ('They are holy angels...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide ritual sepulture and lasting reverence at tombs for heroes and outstandingly good citizens; extend similar honours to exceptionally virtuous persons who die other than in battle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spare fellow Hellenes from slavery
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘No Hellene should be owned by them as a slave; that is a rule which they will observe and advise the other Hellenes to observe.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid enslaving fellow members of the cultural/political community (Hellenes). This fosters unity against external enemies and prevents internecine weakening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not despoil the dead; allow burial
rubrics_metrics.description: Conquerors ought to take nothing but the armour; they must abstain from spoiling the dead or hindering their burial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plunder of corpses encourages cowardice and is morally mean ('illiberality and avarice'); forbidding such acts upholds honour and prevents soldiers from shirking battle in hope of loot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not dedicate spoils of kin at temples
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Neither shall we offer up arms at the temples of the gods, least of all the arms of Hellenes, if we care to maintain good feeling with other Hellenes...’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid dedicating captured arms of fellow Hellenes as temple offerings, since such offerings risk pollution and damage relations, unless explicitly commanded by the god.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forbid devastation and house-burning in internal conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: When Hellenes fight one another (discord), the practice of devastating lands or burning houses should be forbidden; take only the annual produce and no more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish war (external) from discord (internal). In internal quarrels, limit harm to economically necessary measures and avoid scorched-earth tactics that rend the polity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat internal opponents as correctors, not enemies
rubrics_metrics.description: In conflicts among citizens they will use friendly correction but will not enslave or destroy their opponents; enmity is to be treated as discord among friends and not perpetual war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for reconciliation: punish or compel the guilty few but avoid collective punishment of the many; practices should presume common bonds and seek restoration rather than annihilation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit spoils-taking to avoid encouraging cowardice
rubrics_metrics.description: Taking plunder from the dead affords an excuse for not facing the battle; cowards skulk about the dead, pretending to fulfil duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy should avoid incentives (loot) that reward shirking of civic/military duty. Practical rule: restrict permissible booty to reduce shirking and disorder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow women to serve as military auxiliaries or in ranks when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: If you suppose the women to join their armies, whether in the same rank or in the rear, either as a terror to the enemy, or as auxiliaries in case of need, I know that they will then be absolutely invincible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be open to including women in military roles (front or rear) when this strengthens the city's defence; inclusion here is presented as a pragmatic advantage, not token.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophers (or philosophic rulers) must govern
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Until philosophers are kings, or the kings and princes of this world have the spirit and power of philosophy, and political greatness and wisdom meet in one... cities will never have rest from their evils.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political authority must be combined with philosophical wisdom; ruling by those lacking knowledge of the good leads to persistent civic ills. This is a structural political prescription: those who govern should grasp higher truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of true philosopher — lover of whole wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: The philosopher is a lover, not of a part of wisdom only, but of the whole; he desires the whole class of goods and the sight of absolute beauty/being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate true philosophers (seekers of absolute forms) from those who love particular pleasures or partial knowledges (lovers of opinion). The ruler must be of the former sort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophers must grasp absolute being (forms), not mere opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge corresponds to being (the eternal, unchangeable); opinion corresponds to the intermediate flux of the many. Philosophers can see the absolute and eternal and therefore 'know' rather than merely opine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rulers should possess the intellectual capacity to apprehend unchanging principles (the Good, Beauty, Justice) rather than relying on variable appearances or popular opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Love of truth (truthfulness) is essential
rubrics_metrics.description: They will never intentionally receive into their mind falsehood, which is their detestation, and they will love the truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Truthfulness is intrinsic to the philosophical nature and a necessary moral/intellectual quality for rulers; loving wisdom implies hating falsehood—anti-pattern: those who accept falsehood cannot be genuine guardians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperance and absence of covetousness
rubrics_metrics.description: He whose desires are drawn towards knowledge in every form will be absorbed in the pleasures of the soul, and will hardly feel bodily pleasure... Such an one is sure to be temperate and the reverse of covetous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical rulers should have restrained bodily appetites and lack greed for wealth or honors, reducing conflicts of interest and corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnificence of mind; freedom from meanness and fear of death
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be no secret corner of illiberality; nothing can be more antagonistic than meanness to a soul which is ever longing after the whole of things... Or can such an one account death fearful?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A true philosopher is magnanimous, not petty or mean, and is not ruled by fear of death—qualities that enable bold, disinterested leadership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice, gentleness and sociability as signs of philosophical nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Can he ever be unjust or hard in his dealings? Impossible... you will soon observe whether a man is just and gentle, or rude and unsociable; these are the signs which distinguish even in youth the philosophical nature from the unphilosophical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical markers of suitability: fairness, kindness, and agreeable social behavior (observable even in youth) versus rudeness or unsociability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure in learning and good memory
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether he has or has not a pleasure in learning; and again, if he is forgetful and retains nothing of what he learns, will he not be an empty vessel?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A guardian should enjoy study and retain learning (good memory). Lack of retention or joy in learning indicates unsuitability for philosophic training and office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-proportioned, harmonious character
rubrics_metrics.description: The inharmonious and unseemly nature can only tend to disproportion... Then, besides other qualities, we must try to find a naturally well-proportioned and gracious mind, which will move spontaneously towards the true being of everything.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character harmony and proportion (aesthetic/ethical balance) are signs of souls fit for knowledge and rulership; proportion is linked to truth and good judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guardians must possess knowledge to guard laws and institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The guardian who is to keep anything should have eyes rather than no eyes’ ... those wanting in the knowledge of the true being of each thing are simply blind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those entrusted with custody of law and order must have genuine understanding (not merely experience or habit); without true knowledge they cannot properly order or preserve the polity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rulers must be perfected by education and age—union of excellences
rubrics_metrics.description: To men like him, when perfected by years and education, and to these only you will entrust the State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophic ruling requires long education and maturation: only those who combine the enumerated virtues and have been formed by training and time should govern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rulers as skilled 'pilots' (expertise justifies authority)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parable: the true pilot must pay attention to year and seasons and sky and stars and winds, and must and will be the steerer, whether other people like or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority should rest on demonstrable technical/artistic knowledge (political 'navigation'), not on popularity or force; anti-pattern: crews (sailors) claiming control without skill, rewarding demagoguery.
